course_information.title: Time Management & Prioritization
course_information.description: Prioritize customer needs, safety, assigned work, interruptions, and shift handoffs in a busy hardware store.
course_information.scope: General independent hardware retail; store-specific rules are not supplied
course_information.restrictions: No legal, tax, HR, accounting, or licensed-professional advice. Follow store procedures and refer restricted decisions.
learning_objectives: Distinguish urgent work from important planned work.
Choose safe priorities when several tasks compete.
Break a task into a practical next step.
Respond to interruptions without losing track of work.
Use brief handoffs and checklists to support follow-through.

lessons.title: Recognize Priorities During a Shift
lessons.objective: Identify which tasks need attention first.
lessons.why_this_matters: Hardware stores have customer questions, deliveries, and planned work happening at the same time.

content_sections.heading: Safety comes first
content_sections.text: A spill, blocked emergency exit, or other immediate hazard needs prompt action under store procedure. Do not walk past a hazard to finish routine stocking.

content_sections.heading: Consider urgency and importance
content_sections.text: An urgent issue needs attention soon. Important work supports service and operations even when no one is asking about it right now.

content_sections.heading: Confirm the order
content_sections.text: When priorities compete, tell the manager what is happening and ask which task should come next.

lessons.hardware_store_example: You are restocking screws when you notice liquid on the floor. Secure the area and follow spill procedures before returning to the shelf.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “I found a spill. I’m following the safety procedure, then I’ll return to stocking.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Treating the longest task as most important; ignoring hazards; silently dropping assigned work.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask for help with hazardous spills, injuries, or competing demands you cannot resolve safely.

lessons.title: Plan the Next Useful Step
lessons.objective: Turn a broad task into manageable actions.
lessons.why_this_matters: A clear next step helps employees start and finish work.

content_sections.heading: Define the outcome
content_sections.text: Instead of “fix receiving,” identify the specific result, such as sorting today’s delivery into labeled staging areas.

content_sections.heading: Break work into steps
content_sections.text: Check instructions, gather supplies, complete one section, and verify the result. Use a short checklist when several details matter.

content_sections.heading: Estimate realistically
content_sections.text: Ask about deadlines and available time. Do not promise a completion time without considering interruptions and resources.

lessons.hardware_store_example: An associate is told to prepare an endcap. They check the approved display plan, gather products and labels, build the display, and request a final check.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “I’ll gather the products and labels first, then set the display and verify the prices.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Starting without instructions; doing easy tasks instead of required tasks; skipping verification.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask a manager when the assignment, display rules, or available time is unclear.

lessons.title: Handle Interruptions Without Losing Your Place
lessons.objective: Respond to customers while keeping track of unfinished work.
lessons.why_this_matters: Helping a customer should not mean forgetting a half-completed task.

content_sections.heading: Pause safely
content_sections.text: Put down tools and materials safely. Do not leave sharp objects, unstable stacks, or open cartons where customers could be hurt.

content_sections.heading: Capture your place
content_sections.text: Use a permitted checklist or brief note to mark the next step. Never record unnecessary customer personal information.

content_sections.heading: Return or hand off
content_sections.text: After helping, resume from the note. If the shift changes or a new priority takes over, tell the next person what remains.

lessons.hardware_store_example: While checking shelf labels, a customer asks for help finding a faucet connector. You make the area safe, mark the aisle section you were checking, and return after assisting.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “I’m helping this customer. I’ve marked where I stopped so I can finish the label check.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Leaving trip hazards; relying on memory for many unfinished tasks; refusing reasonable customer help.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask a coworker or manager when multiple customers need help or a safety-sensitive task cannot be paused.

lessons.title: Communicate When Priorities Change
lessons.objective: Tell the right person when work must be rescheduled.
lessons.why_this_matters: A silent change can leave important tasks unfinished.

content_sections.heading: Give a short update
content_sections.text: State what was planned, what interrupted it, and what remains. Keep the update factual and concise.

content_sections.heading: Ask for a decision
content_sections.text: If two tasks cannot both be completed, ask the responsible leader which has priority. Do not guess when a deadline or safety concern matters.

content_sections.heading: Use teamwork
content_sections.text: Request a handoff or help when appropriate. Share enough context for the other person to continue without starting over.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A delivery arrives while you are setting a promotional display. You tell the manager the display is half finished and ask whether to help receive the truck.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “The display needs about one more section. The truck is here. Which should I handle first?”
lessons.common_mistakes: Pretending both tasks are done; changing priorities without notice; blaming others for unclear handoffs.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate missed deadlines, customer commitments, or work requiring special authorization.

lessons.title: Close the Shift with a Useful Handoff
lessons.objective: Leave clear information for the next employee.
lessons.why_this_matters: Good handoffs prevent repeated work and missed customer promises.

content_sections.heading: Record what is done
content_sections.text: Check off completed tasks and confirm any important results, such as corrected shelf labels or received cartons.

content_sections.heading: Name what remains
content_sections.text: List unfinished tasks, location, urgency, and any relevant next step. Follow approved systems and privacy rules.

content_sections.heading: Confirm ownership
content_sections.text: Tell the incoming employee or manager who will take the next action. Do not assume a note alone guarantees follow-through.

lessons.hardware_store_example: At shift change, you report that aisle four is stocked but two labels need printing, and you identify where the label request was saved.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Aisle four is stocked. Two labels are pending in the approved system, and the next shift has the request.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Saying only “not done”; leaving customer promises undocumented; sharing private details in open notes.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate urgent safety issues and time-sensitive customer commitments directly, not only in a written note.

options.B: Completed work, unfinished items, and who owns the next step
options.C: Private customer details unrelated to the task
